studies.title: There Is Nothing Like Him
studies.meaning: Two halves that look mismatched are doing one job. The first describes making and increase: mates from among yourselves, pairs among the animals, and a verb meaning to scatter seed, which is how the multiplying is pictured. Then the sentence turns and denies likeness altogether. The commentators discuss the doubled construction in the Arabic, which places two words for resemblance side by side, and generally read the repetition as strengthening the denial. Two names follow at once, and they keep the denial from producing distance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just said that God could have made people a single community and did not, and that whatever people differ about returns to Him for judgement. This ayah states the ground underneath all of that. In Mecca the objects of devotion were imagined on a human scale, with lineages, preferences and rivalries, so a sentence removing likeness entirely cut against the way divinity was ordinarily pictured.

keyTerms.note: A farming verb for broadcasting seed by hand across a field. Applied to human increase, it counts people the way a grower counts a crop, which is why it follows the mention of pairs.
Two words for resemblance placed together, one meaning like and one meaning the likeness of. Grammarians have debated the construction for centuries and generally treat the doubling as emphasis.

An intensive form, not a description of an organ. Placed immediately after likeness is denied, it prevents the denial from being read as remoteness, since hearing implies a listener close enough to be addressed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Increase was how wealth was counted. Seed went out by hand across a field and was measured at harvest; animals were paired deliberately and the year's lambs and calves were tallied against the last. A household's future was the size of that number. The verb this ayah uses for human multiplying is the one a farmer used, which places people inside the same accounting as the flocks.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause denying likeness contains two separate words for resemblance in a row, which by ordinary grammar would produce the odd sense of nothing being like His likeness. Classical grammarians have written on the construction at length and generally hold that the doubling intensifies rather than qualifies, so the denial is stronger and not weaker for it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The denial sits in the middle of the description rather than at its end, and so governs what stands on both sides of it. Making and pairing are described, likeness is refused, hearing and seeing are affirmed. The order is doing the work: the refusal stops the earlier images from being assembled into a portrait, and the two names stop the refusal from producing a God too abstract to address.

crossReferences.why: Closes the shortest statement of the same point with a denial of anything comparable to Him.
Puts the limit in terms of sight, vision unable to grasp Him while He grasps vision entirely.
Names the practice this ayah rules out, coining comparisons for God out of what is at hand.

studies.applyIt: Notice the picture you are using the next time you address God: a direction, a height, a face, a presence with a shape. Everyone has one. Set it down for the length of a single prayer and speak anyway. This ayah does not offer a better picture. It removes the category and then says He hears you.

studies.title: I Ask Of You No Wage
studies.meaning: The messenger states that he asks no payment, and then names an exception, and it is the exception the commentators record several readings of. Some take it as affection within kinship generally, so that what is asked is that people keep their family ties. Some take it as affection toward the near relatives of the one bringing the message. Some read it as drawing near to God through good work. The classical sources set the range out without collapsing it. The clause that follows is not disputed at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Refusing a wage is something the Quran's prophets say repeatedly, each to his own people, and the objection it answers was live in Mecca, where any new public voice was assumed to be speaking for a paymaster. The surah has just described people who want the harvest of this world. Commentators differ over this ayah's placement, some treating it as Medinan inside a Meccan surah, and they do not settle it.

keyTerms.note: Connected to the word for skin, because news shows in a face before it is spoken. The verb names the delivery of good news specifically, and its opposite is used for warning.
An abstract noun for closeness that the Quran uses for relatives. Because it names the relation rather than the people, the phrase built on it can be read in more than one direction.
Usually used of acquiring a wrong, from a root meaning to scrape together. Applying it to a good deed is deliberate, and it keeps the sense of something gathered by effort rather than received.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man who spoke publicly in Arabia was assumed to be speaking for someone: a patron, a clan, or his own advancement. Poets were commissioned. Soothsayers charged fees. The first question asked about any new voice was who was funding it and what they wanted. In that setting a public refusal of payment was not a pious flourish but a claim anyone could test over time.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence about asking no wage is repeated, in almost identical words, by five different prophets within a single surah of the Quran. Noah, then Hud, Salih, Lot and Shu'ayb each say it to their own people in turn, so the refusal of payment is presented as a recurring mark of the office rather than a personal choice.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The clause everyone agrees on is the one about increase, and it describes something more than a larger payment: the goodness of the deed itself is enlarged. The refusal of a wage matters in a different way. It removes the one motive that would make the message a transaction, and it is placed in the messenger's own mouth rather than asserted about him by someone else.

crossReferences.why: Gives the first of the five identical refusals in that surah, spoken by Noah to his own people.
Repeats the refusal and names what the message is instead: a reminder for all the worlds.
States the increase this ayah promises, a good deed multiplied and no one wronged by an atom's weight.

studies.applyIt: Contact one relative you have not spoken to in a year and have nothing to ask them. No news to deliver, no favour, no occasion. Five minutes. Every reading the commentators give of this ayah has affection and nearness in it somewhere, and the version nearest to hand is usually the one that has been left longest.

studies.title: And He Pardons Much
studies.meaning: A hard sentence followed by a clause that is easy to read past: whatever strikes you comes of what your hands earned, and He pardons much. The commentators place real weight on the second half, several noting that without it the first would describe a world of exact settlement in which every difficulty could be read backwards as a verdict. The word for pardoning means effacing, wiping a mark off a surface. Then the passage moves to ships standing in the sea like landmarks, held up by nothing the passengers arranged.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayat just before describe provision measured out precisely, because unlimited provision would produce excess, and rain sent down after people have given up expecting it. The surah is arguing that what looks like restriction is calibration. This passage extends the argument to misfortune, and the ships lead directly into a warning two lines later that the wind could simply be stilled.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to hit a target. The word treats a misfortune as something aimed and landing rather than as an accident, which is why the sentence can then ask where it came from.
The root means to wipe out a trace, and was used of wind erasing tracks in sand. Pardon in Arabic is therefore a mark removed rather than a penalty waived on a record that stands.
The plural covers both a raised marker and a mountain, and travellers navigated by such things. Ships are described by the one thing on a flat horizon that tells you where you are.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both images came from navigation. Wind effaced tracks in sand within hours, which is why the word for pardoning was a picture from the desert rather than from a court or a ledger. And a ship on the Red Sea rose above a flat horizon so that it could be seen from a long way off, standing where the raised stones stood that guided caravans across country without a road.
studies.didYouKnow: The three-word clause about pardoning much occurs twice within five ayat here. It appears in this passage attached to misfortune, and again a few lines later attached to the same ships, which are said to be wreckable for what their passengers have earned, and then are not. The same phrase closes two different arguments in one stretch of text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage affirms a connection between conduct and consequence and refuses an exact accounting in this life, which are usually offered as alternatives. Because much is pardoned, nobody can read their circumstances backwards into a verdict about themselves or anyone else. The ships then make the same point structurally: what is holding you up is not the thing you assumed was holding you up.

crossReferences.why: States the consequence of exact settlement, that nothing living would be left on the surface of the earth.
Draws the same connection between what hands earn and what surfaces in the world, with a stated purpose.
Repeats the pardon clause a few lines later, applied to the same ships and what could happen to them.

studies.applyIt: Take one difficulty you are currently in and refuse, for today only, both of the explanations you usually reach for: that you brought it on yourself, and that it is arbitrary. Sit with it unexplained for a day. This passage puts a large clause of pardon between the cause and the effect, and that clause is precisely what makes the reading impossible.

studies.title: Whoever Pardons And Puts Right
studies.meaning: Two things are set out in one sentence and the order is deliberate. First a ceiling: the repayment of a wrong is a wrong equal to it, which caps redress at equivalence and closes off escalation. Then an alternative that is offered rather than required, and it has two parts. Whoever pardons and puts things right has his reward with God. The commentators notice that the second verb is not forgoing but repairing, so what is described is reconstruction rather than silence. The closing clause explains why the ceiling exists.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah sits inside a run describing the community's own qualities: they answer their Lord, keep the prayer, decide their affairs by consultation among themselves, spend from what they are given, forgive when angry, and defend themselves when wronged. This line stands between the last two and holds both of them. The surah takes its name from a single word in that list.

keyTerms.note: A return that corresponds to what preceded it, used equally of reward and of penalty. The word already contains the idea of proportion, which the phrase after it then states explicitly.
Exact equivalence, not an approximation. Placing it immediately after the word for recompense sets a ceiling rather than a floor, which is the reverse of how feuds actually worked.
From the root of soundness and repair, used of mending a thing that has broken. Joined to pardon, it describes rebuilding a relation rather than merely declining to press a claim.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Vengeance in Arabia rarely stayed level. A killing was answered by killing someone of greater standing, and feuds ran for generations because each side settled at a premium and the other then owed the difference. Poets recorded and inflamed them, naming the dead in verse that travelled. In that setting a limit of exact equivalence was not leniency. It was the first thing capable of stopping a cycle.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah takes its name from one word inside the list of qualities just above this ayah, describing a community that settles its affairs by mutual consultation. The name comes from a method rather than from a doctrine, a narrative or an opening letter, which makes it unusual among the surah names in use.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A ceiling is set and then a door is opened above it. Equivalence is named as the limit of what redress may reach, and pardon joined to repair is placed in a different economy, with the reward held by God rather than paid by the person who did the wrong. The final clause does quiet work on the injured party, since going past the measure would move them across the line it draws.

crossReferences.why: States the same equivalence and then adds that patience would be better for those who are patient.
Presses pardon by an argument from self-interest: would you not love that God should forgive you?
Places patience joined to forgiveness among the matters of firm resolve, three ayat later.

studies.applyIt: Take a grievance you are genuinely entitled to press. Then ask what putting it right would actually involve, as distinct from being owed for it: a conversation, a thing replaced, a relation resumed. Write the two answers separately. This ayah names two verbs, and most of us do only the first one and call it the second.

studies.title: No Blame On Those Wronged
studies.meaning: Three short ayat holding two things at once. Someone who takes redress after being wronged has no case standing against them, and the case lies instead with those who wrong people and overreach in the land. Then the last line moves, without contradicting either, to the other option: whoever is patient and forgives, that belongs to the firm resolve of matters. The commentators read the balance carefully. The right to answer is protected in the first two ayat precisely so that the forgiveness in the third can be a choice.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage closes a section describing the community's own qualities, and the sequence is unusual: self-defence, then a limit of exact equivalence, then pardon, then the right to redress again, then patience. That layering suggests an audience under real pressure and needing both permissions at once, which fits the situation in Mecca, where believers were being harmed and had little power to answer anything.

keyTerms.note: From the root of help and victory, in a form meaning to obtain that for oneself. It covers seeking justice as well as striking back, and the Arabic does not separate the two here.
Literally a road. The idiom means a route by which someone can be reached with a claim, so denying a way against a person is denying anyone standing to bring one.
Settled intention that has hardened into commitment. The phrase built on it names the things that require it, and the Quran uses the same phrase in only a few places.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing was defended publicly or lost publicly. A man who did not answer a wrong lost the presumption that his household was protected, and others adjusted their behaviour toward him within days. Redress in that world was not personal satisfaction; it was the mechanism by which a family remained safe to live among neighbours. That makes the third of these ayat expensive in a way a modern reader can easily miss.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase in the last ayah for what belongs to firm resolve appears in only a few places in the Quran. One of them is a father's counsel to his son, where it closes a list of prayer, calling to what is right, forbidding wrong and patience under what befalls you. The same words mark two very different things at the top of the same scale.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two positions usually treated as alternatives are held together. A wronged person's right to answer is protected, and stepping past it is described as strength rather than as weakness or as loss. The ordering carries the argument: forgiveness is presented as an act available to someone who had the option and did not need it, which is a different thing entirely from the resignation of someone who never had one.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase for firm resolve, closing a father's list of what to hold to under pressure.
Attaches the same phrase to patience under abuse from others, in a passage about being tested.
Sets the ceiling this passage assumes, redress capped at exact equivalence with pardon above it.

studies.applyIt: Think of one wrong you could still answer and have not. Decide in actual words which of the two you are doing: choosing to let it go, or lacking the means to act. Both are honest positions. Only one of them is what this passage calls resolve, and the difference is invisible from outside and obvious from inside.
